The rule would apply going forward and also to past periods when a port district made employer payments to one of those plans.
WA-2025-SB5905.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5905-S HBA APP 26, 2026-02-17)

WA-2025-SB5906.s: This bill would limit what early learning providers and school district employees may collect about students and family members’ immigration or citizenship status. It would also bar immigration enforcement from nonpublic areas in early learning sites, schools, health care facilities, adult family homes, colleges, and places where ballots are handled unless there is a valid judicial warrant or court order. The bill would require policies and training in these settings and direct contact with a worker’s collective bargaining representative in some cases. It would also require county auditors to mark ballot-handling areas as nonpublic during elections.

WA-2025-SB5911.s: This law changes how the Department of Children, Youth, and Families handles money for people in extended foster care, which means people age 18 to 21 in the department’s care. Beginning January 1, 2027, the department may not use benefits, payments, funds, or accrual paid to or for a person in extended foster care as reimbursement for the cost of care. It also requires the department to check whether a person in extended foster care is eligible for social security benefits and to help with setting up and managing accounts for those benefits.

WA-2025-SB5912.s: The bill would bring back a state task force to study Washington’s system for providing lawyers to people who cannot afford one. It would review how different parts of the state handle these cases, look at delays and staffing needs, and study funding and data issues. The task force would report its findings and recommendations to the Governor, the state Supreme Court, and legislative committees by January 1, 2028.
WA-2025-SB5912.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (5912-S.E SBR APS2 26, 2026-02-09)

WA-2025-SB5915.s: The law changes how Washington reviews health technology for coverage. It gives extra priority to some treatments already used or recommended under Medicare or in expert treatment guides, including those from specialty doctor groups or patient groups. For life-threatening or rare diseases, reviewers must look at all relevant clinical trials and can also consider expert input that some trial design would not be ethical or practical. The law takes effect June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB5915.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5915 HBR APH 26, 2026-03-04)

WA-2025-SB5916.s: The bill would require health plans and managed care organizations to cover at least one FDA-approved nonopioid drug for pain treatment or management without prior authorization or step therapy. It would also require the state health authority to make sure prescription drug practices for fee-for-service programs and managed care organizations meet that rule. By January 1, 2027, the department would have to publish an educational pamphlet about nonopioid alternatives for pain, including drugs and other therapies and their advantages and disadvantages.

WA-2025-SB5917.s: The law expands who can receive abortion medicines from the state health department, including some Indian health providers and urban Indian health groups. It tells the Department of Corrections to work with the Department of Health to find the right recipients and to give out these medicines in bulk when possible. It also removes a past price cap and lets the department charge nothing or some payment for handling and delivery.
WA-2025-SB5917.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (5917-S SBR APS 26, 2026-02-10)

WA-2025-SB5919.s: Fire districts and insurance providers would be encouraged to work together on optional incentives for wildfire safety practices tied to agricultural activities. The incentives would be voluntary for insurance providers to offer and for policyholders to accept. The bill lists examples such as defensible space or fire breaks, proper equipment storage, water tanks, certain farm equipment, and notice of local red flag warnings.
WA-2025-SB5919.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (5919 SBR BTE TA 26, 2026-01-14)

WA-2025-SB5922.s: School districts may ask the state school agency for permission to move money from a student transportation vehicle fund to another fund if they choose not to replace a vehicle and reduce their fleet. The money can include depreciation payments and interest from a fully paid-off vehicle. The law takes effect on 6/11/2026.
WA-2025-SB5922.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5922 HBR APH 26, 2026-03-04)

WA-2025-SB5923.s: A hospital on an island in Skagit County could qualify for critical access hospital payment if it is certified by CMS, the federal Medicare agency. It became law as Chapter 84, 2026 Laws, and takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB5923.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5923-S HBR APP 26, 2026-03-02)

WA-2025-SB5924.s: Starting December 1, 2027, pharmacists would be able to prescribe certain vaccines, addiction medicines, epinephrine pens, allergy medicine, tobacco quit products, HIV prevention medicine, tuberculosis test products, birth control hormones, and some travel-related drugs. They could also prescribe some drugs, drug groups, and devices for minor health problems, as well as some test-guided or team-based care items. The bill also expands the meaning of pharmacy practice and lets the state board make rules to carry out these changes.
WA-2025-SB5924.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (5924-S SBR APS 26, 2026-02-17)

WA-2025-SB5925.s: The bill expands when the attorney general’s office may use civil investigative demands, which are formal written requests for records, questions, or testimony. It lets the office use them in certain possible cases involving state or federal law, labor pay laws, discrimination, jail rules, and related state rules, if an assistant attorney general reviews and approves the demand. It also sets rules for what a demand must say, limits some uses, and says it cannot be used for criminal cases or for federal agencies acting in their official work. It became law as Chapter 243, 2026 Laws, and takes effect on 6/11/2026.
WA-2025-SB5925.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (5925-S.E SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-17)

WA-2025-SB5928.s: The bill would require property insurers that use wildfire risk scores to give policyholders written, plain-language details when a policy is nonrenewed, canceled, or when the score raises premiums. It would also let a policyholder ask once per policy period for a revised score or appeal an inaccurate score if they can show risk-reducing work on the property or nearby community. Insurers would have set times to acknowledge and answer an appeal, and they could have to send appeal records to the Office of the Insurance Commissioner.
WA-2025-SB5928.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5928-S.E HBA CPB 26, 2026-02-23)

WA-2025-SB5931.s: The bill would change how the Workforce Education Investment Accountability and Oversight Board works. It would require the board to pick co-chairs every two years, meet at least four times a year, and send yearly recommendations to the Legislature by December 31. The board would also have to consult with the Washington Student Achievement Council when reviewing whether these education investments are helping students succeed and get ready for jobs, and it would no longer have to keep a public data dashboard.
WA-2025-SB5931.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5931-S HBR PEW 26, 2026-02-27)

WA-2025-SB5936.s: The bill would let a business be held responsible if it knowingly takes part in human trafficking or involuntary servitude, or if it does not stop an employee or agent from doing so in a known pattern for the business's benefit. If a business is prosecuted, a court could also order a fine of up to $1 million per offense, take away profits from that conduct, and bar the business from state and local contracts. It would also require police and prosecutors to keep victims' names, photos, and images private, and to quickly help eligible people get the papers needed for T or U visas, which are federal visas for certain crime victims.
WA-2025-SB5936.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (5936 SBA LAW 26, 2026-01-19)

WA-2025-SB5937.s: The law changes rules for smart entry systems in rental housing. On a tenant’s request, a landlord must offer an alternative key, like a key fob, key card, physical key, or keypad code, that does not use biometrics or a phone app. It also limits what data smart entry systems may collect and use for building, elevator, common area, and unit access. The law takes effect on 1/1/2027.
WA-2025-SB5937.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5937-S.E HBR APH 26, 2026-03-03)

WA-2025-SB5938.s: This law sets a foreclosure prevention fee of $80 for most residential mortgage loans tied to property in Washington. The fee is paid at closing and can be financed in the loan, with some loans exempt, including reverse mortgage loans made to people 60 or older and certain chattel loans or retail installment contracts. For some home purchase loans using certain state homeownership programs, the fee may be collected only on the first lien mortgage loan. The borrower must also be given notice of the fee and its purpose.

WA-2025-SB5941.s: By January 1, 2027, the state energy code would be changed to exempt some school districts in listed counties with 500 or fewer students from having to add a renewable energy system in certain new school buildings or additions over 10,000 square feet. The exemption would apply to school districts in the listed eastern and central Washington counties. If a district gets this exemption, the council could not require extra energy-saving steps just because of it.
WA-2025-SB5941.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5941-S HBA LG 26, 2026-02-16)

WA-2025-SB5944.s: The law changes collective bargaining for language access providers, and it says payments or reimbursements for missed or canceled appointments count as economic compensation that must be bargained. If a rule, policy, or executive order on wages, hours, or working conditions conflicts with the agreement, the agreement controls. If an agreement conflicts with state law, the conflicting part of the agreement is not valid. It became law and takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB5944.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5944 HBA LAWS 26, 2026-02-16)

WA-2025-SB5947.s: This bill would establish the Washington health care board and give it 19 members appointed by the governor. The board would design the Washington health plan, hire staff, study how to carry it out, and make recommendations to the legislature. The plan is meant to provide all medically necessary health care services for all residents of the state, but it could not be implemented until federal waiver and funding conditions are met.

WA-2025-SB5956.s: This bill would set limits on how public schools use artificial intelligence, automated decision systems, and surveillance technologies. It would bar schools from using these tools as the only or deciding reason for student discipline, and from using them to make predictive risk scores or watchlists based only on automated systems. It would also limit the use of biometric data, restrict disclosure of student personal information to law enforcement, and ban school district use of facial recognition for ongoing surveillance or real-time tracking of students. The bill would also require updated state guidance and a model policy for school districts, charter schools, and state-tribal education compact schools.

WA-2025-SB5957.s: The law expands the Homeless Youth Advisory Committee to add more members with lived experience of homelessness or of public systems like child welfare, behavioral health, juvenile justice, or youth homelessness programs. It also lets youth or young adult members serve if they are under 25, and lets a member who turns 25 finish the term. The law takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB5957.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5957 HBR ELHS 26, 2026-02-27)

WA-2025-SB5961.s: This bill would move the imagination library program from the Department of Children, Youth, and Families to the Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction. OSPI would select a Washington-based nonprofit to run the program, and that nonprofit would work with a national nonprofit foundation to mail books each month to eligible children from birth to age five at no cost to families. The selected nonprofit would also report on affiliate programs and child enrollment each year. OSPI would contract with a nonprofit experienced in promoting early literacy for children through pediatric office visits.

WA-2025-SB5963.s: Starting in the 2026-27 school year, a student who qualifies for the Passport to Careers program would also count as income-eligible for the Washington College Grant. The bill changes how financial need is figured for Passport to Careers, using the gap between a student’s school cost and their student aid index, a federal measure of aid need. It also requires the Office of Student Financial Assistance to put all Passport to Careers money into the State Financial Aid Account. It became law and takes effect on 6/11/2026.
WA-2025-SB5963.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (5963 SBR FBR 26, 2026-03-30)

WA-2025-SB5968.s: This bill would update Washington law on permitting and licensing by folding executive order 25-03 into chapter 43.42A RCW. It would require agencies with enough resources to track and report more data on credential applications, including application counts, pending and backlog applications, and processing times. It would also require the office to maintain a statewide credential catalog and central online repository of credential information for applicants.

WA-2025-SB5969.s: This law changes how high school and beyond plans work for students with individualized education programs. It requires those plans to be aligned with the student’s transition plan and linked to the statewide online individualized education program system to reduce duplication. It also requires the superintendent to maintain that online system and provide training and technical help for educators, administrators, and families.

WA-2025-SB5970.s: The bill would make the property tax exemption for multipurpose senior citizen centers permanent. It would keep that exemption from ending under the automatic ten-year expiration.
WA-2025-SB5970.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (5970 SBA WM 26, 2026-01-15)

WA-2025-SB5971.s: The Washington State Department of Agriculture would create a green fertilizer incentive program to support making and using low-carbon nitrogen fertilizer in the state. The program could offer rebates, grants, and other payments or support to farmers, fertilizer makers and sellers, tribal governments, and agricultural co-ops. The department would submit a report by December 1, 2027, and the program would take effect after that report is delivered and the Legislature gives money for it.
WA-2025-SB5971.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5971-S HBA AGNR 26, 2026-02-23)

WA-2025-SB5972.s: The bill would expand who can use interest arbitration, which is a process for settling contract disputes. It would remove the size limit that only let jail correctional employees in counties over 70,000 people qualify. It would apply to uniformed and non-uniformed security staff in jails, including both commissioned and non-commissioned workers.
WA-2025-SB5972.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5972-S HBA LAWS 26, 2026-02-17)

WA-2025-SB5974.s: The law sets new age, background, certification, and work-history rules for people who want to serve as city or town chiefs, marshals, or sheriffs. It also spells out when a vacancy is created if a chief, marshal, or sheriff loses certification or no longer meets the rules, and it says counties or cities must fill that vacancy. It also gives sheriffs added duties to enforce state and federal law and says the law took effect on 4/30/2026.
WA-2025-SB5974.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (5974-S2 SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-20)

WA-2025-SB5975.s: The law sets limits on lead in aluminum or brass cookware, utensils, and cookware components sold in Washington. It bars manufacturers, retailers, and wholesalers from making or selling certain items that have lead above the listed limits, and it gives an exemption for some previously owned sales and nonprofit sales. It also requires the state to give guidance to manufacturers and to treat cookware containing lead as a priority consumer product for further review and possible rules.

WA-2025-SB5977.s: The Department of Children, Youth, and Families would have to publish a report on each child near-fatality review within 180 days after the review ends, unless the Governor grants more time. The report would be sent to lawmakers and posted on the department’s public website, and parts with private information could be blanked out.
WA-2025-SB5977.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5977 HBA ELHS 26, 2026-02-18)

WA-2025-SB5981.s: Washington law now bars drug makers, or others acting for them, from blocking or limiting certain 340B drug deliveries to covered health care groups, their contract pharmacies, or other approved locations, unless federal law allows it. It also bars them from making those groups share claims or other data just to get the drugs, unless federal law requires it. Covered entities may sue for violations, and the law lets courts award up to $5,000 per day for each violation; it also requires certain hospitals and health centers to report 340B program data to the Health Care Authority. It takes effect on 6/11/2026.
WA-2025-SB5981.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (5981-S2.E SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-16)

WA-2025-SB5982.s: This law updates parts of the clean energy transformation act for consumer-owned utilities, including port districts. It changes several definitions used in the law, including "consumer-owned utility," "market customer," and "affected market customer." The changes affect utilities that distribute electricity and electricity users who buy power from other entities or generate electricity for their own use.

WA-2025-SB5984.s: This bill would create rules for artificial intelligence companion chatbots in Washington. Operators would have to clearly tell users the chatbot is artificial, repeat that notice during longer chats, and stop chatbots from claiming to be human. For minors, operators would also have to block sexually explicit content, limit manipulative engagement tactics, and give the notice more often. Operators would also need a protocol for detecting and responding to suicidal ideation or self-harm and publicly disclose details of that protocol.

WA-2025-SB5985.s: This bill would direct the University of Washington, with Washington State University and other stakeholders, to create and maintain an online resource center with information about endometriosis. The resource center would include information on awareness, incidence, prevalence, diagnosis, care, and how health care professionals talk with patients about endometriosis. The bill would also require the Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction to add menstrual health information, including how to tell normal menstrual discomfort from severe symptoms that may need medical attention such as endometriosis, when revising state health and physical education standards.

WA-2025-SB5988.s: The law lets Washington’s health department ask for federal approval to provide accreditation services for opioid treatment programs. It directs the department to set fees for new accreditations and renewals high enough to cover the cost of the service, and it may use money from the Opioid Abatement Settlement Account to help pay those costs. It became law in 2026 and takes effect on 6/11/2026.
WA-2025-SB5988.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (5988 SBR APS 26, 2026-02-13)

WA-2025-SB5992.s: This bill would create the youth development fund account to support youth development programs. The superintendent of public instruction could give grants from the account to nonprofits, tribal governments, and city or county parks and recreation entities, and school districts or educational service districts could apply only in certain cases. The grants would support programs for youth ages five to 24, such as mentoring, learning support, after-school or summer programs, arts, STEM, sports, outdoor education, youth civic engagement, and cultural programming.

WA-2025-SB5993.s: This bill would limit interest on new medical debt accrued after December 31, 2026, to simple interest of 1% per year, before or after a judgment. It would also bar interest from being charged or collected during any period when a hospital has not completed required charity care screening, or when the debt is later found to be invalid, not lawfully owed, or not legally enforceable. Any interest charged on a medical debt that is later reduced, eliminated, or found invalid would be void and must be refunded.

WA-2025-SB5994.s: The law lets school districts keep getting timber tax money for a year even if they do not have a qualifying levy, as long as they had one in either of the two prior years. It uses the highest levy rate from those two years to figure the payment, and it took effect on March 16, 2026.
WA-2025-SB5994.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (5994 SBR WM OC 26, 2026-02-04)

WA-2025-SB5995.s: Port districts and port development authorities would be allowed to keep using money to buy cargo equipment with zero or very low emissions after the current end date. The bill would also keep in place the ban on buying fully automated marine cargo handling equipment. It became law and takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB5995.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (5995 HBR LG 26, 2026-02-23)

WA-2025-SB5998.s: The law changes the state’s 2025-2027 operating budget for various agencies and programs. It affects state government spending on those agencies and programs. It became law on April 1, 2026, and took effect that day.
WA-2025-SB5998.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (5998-S.E SBR HA 26, 2026-03-02)

WA-2025-SB6002.s: The law sets rules for how state and local agencies can use automatic license plate readers. It limits use to certain law enforcement, parking, and traffic jobs, bans use for immigration enforcement and some sensitive places, and requires agencies to register the systems, train users, and delete most data within 21 days. It also says a license plate match alone is not enough for a stop, and the law took effect on March 30, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6002.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6002-S.E SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-17)

WA-2025-SB6003.s: This law changes Washington’s 2025-2027 capital budget, which is the state’s spending plan for buildings and other long-term projects. It affects funding for general government agencies, human services, natural resource agencies, and schools and colleges. It became law on April 1, 2026, and took effect that day.
WA-2025-SB6003.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6003 SBR WM TA 26, 2026-02-25)

WA-2025-SB6005.s: The law changes the 2025-27 state transportation budget for several transportation agencies and programs. It became law on March 31, 2026, and took effect that day.
WA-2025-SB6005.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6005 SBR TRAN TA 26, 2026-02-25)

WA-2025-SB6006.s: Washington would exempt food banks and other food distributing nonprofits from retail sales tax on certain services they buy, such as software, website work, IT support, security, temporary staffing, advertising, live presentations, and some digital processing services. A food distributing organization is a charitable nonprofit that gives food away for free to other nonprofits or the public. The tax break would not be set to expire and would not go through the usual review for tax breaks.
WA-2025-SB6006.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6006 SBA WM 26, 2026-02-13)

WA-2025-SB6007.s: The bill would have the Washington State Institute for Public Policy study how the Department of Children, Youth, and Families uses screening tools for child welfare referrals. The study would look at how those tools affect family assessment responses, voluntary and required services, dependency cases, out-of-home placements, repeat referrals, and child deaths or near deaths. The institute would share preliminary findings by December 1, 2026, and a final report with the Legislature and the department by September 1, 2027.
WA-2025-SB6007.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6007-S HBA APP 26, 2026-02-17)

WA-2025-SB6009.s: This bill changes how some land use decisions are reviewed in court. It allows the superior court to transfer review to the court of appeals if all parties agree and the case can be decided on an existing record. If the case is transferred, the parties give up the right to seek attorneys' fees and costs under the stated law, and a party's refusal to consent cannot be used as evidence.

WA-2025-SB6011.s: The law lets Court of Appeals bailiffs check threats against Court of Appeals judges and staff, and get certain criminal history records for that work. If a threat looks real, they must send it to local law enforcement, which can share updates back with the bailiffs. The court must make sure bailiffs have the right training and experience. It became law and takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6011.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6011 HBA CRJ 26, 2026-02-17)

WA-2025-SB6013.s: The bill would update ski area rules to include aerial tramways, tows, conveyors, and other lift devices in safety and conduct standards. It would require owners or operators to build, maintain, and run these devices so they safely carry patrons, workers, and the public. It would also require operators of aerial tramways, tows, and conveyors, including schools and ski clubs, to keep at least $1 million in liability insurance per accident.
WA-2025-SB6013.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6013 SBR APS 26, 2026-02-05)

WA-2025-SB6014.s: The law expands workplace pregnancy accommodations that an employer cannot refuse as a hardship claim, starting January 1, 2027, and restores the rules that were in place before 2027. It also makes certain complaint records held by the Department of Labor and Industries private if they could identify a worker or job applicant, while still allowing some summary data and limited sharing when needed for an investigation or legal case. The bill became law and takes effect on January 1, 2027.
WA-2025-SB6014.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6014-S HBR APH 26, 2026-03-04)

WA-2025-SB6019.s: The law changes how Washington sets payment rates for home care agencies and how much of those rates must go to worker wages, benefits, and required employer costs. It also sets rules for how the Department of Social and Health Services checks that agencies spent those funds as required, and it lets the department set an admin rate for agency overhead and a training rate for worker training and certification costs. It became law as Chapter 85, 2026 Laws, and takes effect on 6/11/2026.
WA-2025-SB6019.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6019 SBR HLTC OC 26, 2026-01-30)

WA-2025-SB6024.s: This bill would limit the Department of Social and Health Services to no more than one annual routine review per community residential service business provider in certain subject areas. It would also require the department to combine review activities when possible and share documents and records within the department to avoid repeated requests. The limits would not apply to adult protective services investigations, incident reports, complaint investigations, citation follow-up activities, mortality reviews, or other monitoring required by state or federal law.

WA-2025-SB6025.s: The law updates the state’s definition of fetal death. It now covers a fetus with no sign of life after birth that is at least 20 weeks along, or weighs 350 grams if the number of weeks is not known. It became law on March 14, 2026, and takes effect June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6025.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6025 SBR FBR 26, 2026-03-31)

WA-2025-SB6026.s: The law says cities and counties of 30,000 or more people, and other counties that plan under the state growth law, cannot ban homes in areas zoned for commercial or mixed-use development. It also limits when local rules can require mixed-use buildings or ground-floor stores as a condition for allowing housing. The law takes effect on 6/11/2026 and applies to local governments that do not update their rules within 18 months after that date.
WA-2025-SB6026.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6026-S2.E SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-16)

WA-2025-SB6027.s: Washington law changes how certain local taxes for affordable housing and related services can be used. At least 60 percent of one housing tax must go to running and maintaining existing affordable housing, housing-related facilities, or fixing up existing affordable housing, and the rest may go to those uses or rental help. It also expands allowed uses for some housing grant money to cover resident services, basic upkeep, case management, and other support for permanent supportive housing, and it says the state housing agency may not set overhead caps below 15 percent for grantees.
WA-2025-SB6027.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6027-S2.E SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-16)

WA-2025-SB6031.s: The bill would expand Washington’s insurance fraud program to cover more kinds of fraud and other crimes that affect insurers, insurance consumers, and beneficiaries. It would also broaden the training needed for staff who work on these cases and make restitution a goal, meaning offenders may have to pay back money lost in fraud cases. It would redefine insurance fraud and make it a class B felony, including some false claims, fake billing, and false repair or medical records.
WA-2025-SB6031.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6031-S.E HBA CPB 26, 2026-02-24)

WA-2025-SB6034.s: The law makes the Governor’s Office of Indian Affairs a cabinet agency in the governor’s office. It sets the office’s main jobs, including helping state agencies work with federally recognized tribes, giving advice on tribal issues, and meeting with tribal leaders and state officials. The office must also provide training for top state leaders and send an annual report to the governor and Legislature. It became law on March 30, 2026, and takes effect June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6034.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6034-S SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-17)

WA-2025-SB6035.s: The law requires county auditors to meet with federally recognized tribes about voting centers and ballot drop boxes on tribal land, and it sets steps for getting help from the Secretary of State if contact is hard to make. It also requires the Secretary of State to meet with tribes every two years to discuss barriers to voting, including voter outreach, online registration using tribal ID data, and help with tribal-led voter education. The law also covers voting services for military, overseas, Native American, and disabled voters.
WA-2025-SB6035.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6035-S2 SBR HA 26, 2026-03-03)

WA-2025-SB6036.s: The bill would let the state exempt some former foster care providers from getting an adult family home license. To qualify, a person must meet set care history and safety checks, and in some cases can only provide care to the former foster youth who lived with them. It affects certain Washington foster care providers and the adults they care for.
WA-2025-SB6036.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6036-S SBR APS 26, 2026-02-05)

WA-2025-SB6039.s: The law updates how the Department of Labor and Industries can send notices, orders, citations, and other messages. It lets the agency use email or another electronic or paper method, and in some cases the message must be trackable or confirmable. It affects several Labor and Industries programs, including contractor registration, trade licensing, workplace safety, wage and hour rules, workers’ compensation, and equipment inspections. Before using an electronic method for the first time in some cases, the agency must give people a paper option.
WA-2025-SB6039.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6039-S SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-01)

WA-2025-SB6044.s: The bill would name the new moon day of the Hindu month of Kartik, also known as Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas, as a legislatively recognized day in Washington. It affects people who observe these holidays and state recognition of them.
WA-2025-SB6044.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6044 HBA SGOV 26, 2026-02-23)

WA-2025-SB6046.s: Washington created a state Civil Air Patrol unit inside the military department. People who serve in the federal Civil Air Patrol’s Washington wing may volunteer to join the state unit, which can be used for training, communications, cyber security, disaster relief, search and rescue, and related work. The Governor may call it into active state service, and it may work with state and local agencies and federally recognized tribes. It became law and takes effect June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6046.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6046 SBR FBR 26, 2026-03-31)

WA-2025-SB6049.s: This bill would change what employment and licensing records are exempt from public disclosure. It would add exemptions for some personal demographic details, benefit enrollment information, and voluntary survey responses, while still allowing deidentified, anonymized, or aggregated release in some cases. It also keeps certain exam, application, personnel, and investigation records private, and requires notice when records from an employee’s personnel, payroll, supervisor, or training file are requested.

WA-2025-SB6054.s: This law says governing documents for common interest communities may not ban the installation, use, or maintenance of fire-hardened building materials if they meet health, safety, and local permit requirements. The documents may set reasonable rules on design, size, placement, or exterior appearance, but those rules cannot make the materials impossible to use or raise their cost too much. The law also says it does not give a property owner the right to place these materials on someone else’s property, leased property without permission, or common areas. It applies retroactively to existing governing documents, and any conflicting provision is void and unenforceable.

WA-2025-SB6058.s: The law gives the state labor agency more choice in whether to investigate a worker’s wage complaint. If it accepts a complaint, it must act within 60 days unless it gets more time for good cause. It also changes when the time limit for a worker’s court case pauses and lets the agency add civil penalties in some wage cases.
WA-2025-SB6058.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6058 SBR LC OC 26, 2026-02-04)

WA-2025-SB6065.s: This law lets certain school districts take temporary loans from their capital projects fund or transportation vehicle fund if they are under binding conditions or enhanced financial oversight. The loan must be repaid within one year, cannot earn interest, and must be approved by the district board; districts under enhanced oversight also need approval from the special administrator. It also allows the transportation vehicle fund to be used for buying and repairing pupil transportation vehicles, electric or zero-emission charging and fueling stations, and converting gas or diesel vehicles to electric or zero-emission vehicles. In some cases, a district under enhanced financial oversight may ask to move money from the transportation vehicle fund to another school fund, including turning a temporary loan into a permanent transfer without repayment.

WA-2025-SB6066.s: This law lets counties, cities, and towns create crash prevention zones in certain areas, and later in other areas where serious injury or fatal crashes are higher than expected. Before a zone is final, the local government must hold a public hearing and do an engineering and traffic study of the roads in the zone. It also allows more traffic enforcement and automated speed cameras in these zones, and doubles the base penalty for using a personal electronic device while driving in a crash prevention zone. Money collected from those doubled penalties must be used for engineering studies, road signs, and safety improvements in the zone.

WA-2025-SB6070.s: The bill would let police use certain tracking devices by court order in more missing-person cases, including when they are needed to help protect or locate a missing endangered person. The court would have to find that the device is likely to help and that there is probable cause, or a good reason to believe, that it could aid in finding the person. It also limits how police may use or keep data from a cell site simulator device if they do not get court approval within 48 hours or if the request is denied.
WA-2025-SB6070.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6070-S2.E HBR CS 26, 2026-02-27)

WA-2025-SB6076.s: The law creates a new procurement category for public utility district work on clean power, energy storage, and transmission or distribution projects through January 1, 2045. It raises dollar limits for some work done without a contract and changes bidding rules, including allowing electronic bids, more winning bids up to 25% above estimate, and use of a vendor list for some purchases. For cities and other municipalities, some competitive bidding rules can be waived through January 1, 2045 for certain energy projects when strict conditions are met. It became law and takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6076.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6076-S SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-15)

WA-2025-SB6079.s: The bill would create the Strengthen Washington Homes program, a grant program to help pay for wildfire risk mitigation for insurable dwellings. It would let the insurance commissioner run the program and make rules for grants to property owners, contractors, nonprofit organizations, tribes, and some government entities. It would also bar insurers from using wildfire risk to deny property insurance coverage for property with a current wildfire prepared designation, while still allowing other risk factors to be used.

WA-2025-SB6080.s: The bill would let county and city jails choose to hold people in federal custody when space is available. A jail could do this before a contract is in place, but it would have to make a contract with the United States within 180 days of first taking such a person. The contract would need to set a fee of at least the daily bed rate agreed to by local governments, and a jail could also accept someone if it finds a public safety reason to do so.
WA-2025-SB6080.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6080-S SBR APS 26, 2026-02-17)

WA-2025-SB6081.s: Washington’s Department of Licensing would be barred from sharing or showing records of a person’s sex designation change unless the person gives consent for a specific use. The bill also expands privacy rules for driver records and vital records, including some records that could reveal a person’s sex designation, and it limits when the Department of Health can release certain vital records data. It became law on March 16, 2026, and took effect the same day.
WA-2025-SB6081.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6081-S HBR SGOV 26, 2026-02-27)

WA-2025-SB6084.s: This law makes it a class C felony to intentionally vote, or try to vote, more than once in the same Washington election, or to vote in both Washington and another state in the same election. It says an election is the same one when the date is the same, even if the ballots have different races or measures. A special election held with a primary or general election is treated as a separate election, and the law took effect on March 17, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6084.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6084 HBR SGOV 26, 2026-02-27)

WA-2025-SB6086.s: This bill would let Washington Supreme Court bailiffs and court security personnel conduct threat assessments for judicial officers. It would allow them to receive criminal history record information, including nonconviction data, for investigations of threats against judicial officers. Founded threats would have to be referred to local law enforcement, and the law defines which officials count as judicial officers.

WA-2025-SB6087.s: This law expands liability protection for people and groups that donate or give out baby items that are less than five years old, including religious organizations. It also adds strollers and car seats to the list of covered items, and groups that handle car seats must check the car seat’s history, note that they cannot guarantee its safety, and make sure it is not expired or recalled. The law takes effect June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6087.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6087-S.E SBR FBR 26, 2026-03-31)

WA-2025-SB6091.s: Washington law now requires brokers to market residential property to the general public and all other brokers, not just a limited or exclusive group, unless needed to protect the health or safety of the owner or occupant. It also says public marketing does not mean the owner must let people into the home. The new rule must be added to the pamphlet brokers already give to their clients, and a violation can lead to discipline by the state licensing department.
WA-2025-SB6091.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6091-S SBR APS 26, 2026-02-10)

WA-2025-SB6097.s: Federally recognized Indian tribes would be added to the list of groups that may take part in the Conservation Futures program. The program would let these tribes participate in the same way as other eligible entities.
WA-2025-SB6097.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6097-S HBR AGNR 26, 2026-02-26)

WA-2025-SB6102.s: Beginning July 1, 2026, the state would use the fee rate that was in place on July 4, 2025. Before that date, the bill would change how the ambulance transport fund fee is figured and how the add-on payment rate is updated each year. It affects ambulance transport providers that take part in the fee program and the Health Care Authority, which would calculate the rates.
WA-2025-SB6102.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6102 SBR HLTC OC 26, 2026-01-22)

WA-2025-SB6103.s: The law makes Medicaid payments for services at a rural hospital that the federal government has named a rural emergency hospital subject to state funding approval. It applies no matter whether the patient is in managed care or not. It became Chapter 112, 2026 Laws, and takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6103.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6103 HBR APP 26, 2026-03-02)

WA-2025-SB6106.s: This law changes Washington's rules for layoff and business-closing notices. It says some employers must give written notice before a business closing or mass layoff, and it adds a rule that the employment security department and bargaining representatives can receive the names and addresses of affected employees. It also excludes Indian tribes from the definition of employer and makes those employee names and addresses exempt from public disclosure.

WA-2025-SB6110.s: The law narrows the definition of an electric-assisted bicycle so it does not include vehicles that can go over 20 miles per hour on motor power alone or that can be easily changed to no longer fit the e-bike rules. It also directs the Department of Licensing to gather a work group to study and recommend new rules for electric motorcycles. The group must look at how these vehicles should be defined, registered, licensed, and enforced, and at possible age, training, and penalty rules.
WA-2025-SB6110.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6110-S.E SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-13)

WA-2025-SB6113.s: The law makes technical changes to new retail sales tax rules for some services in Washington. It clarifies which services count as information technology, investigation, temporary staffing, live presentations, and certain digital services, and it gives some public-agency services an exemption when they are shared under an interlocal agreement. It also sets a transition period for some existing contracts from October 1, 2025, through March 31, 2026, and says the Department of Revenue must waive some penalties in certain cases. The law took effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6113.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6113-S.E HBA FIN 26, 2026-02-26)

WA-2025-SB6114.s: The bill would define "fixture" and "affixed" for excise tax purposes. It says real property for real estate excise tax would include fixtures, which are items attached to land or buildings in certain ways. It would also let the Department of Revenue make rules to carry out the law.
WA-2025-SB6114.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6114 SBA WM 26, 2026-01-21)

WA-2025-SB6129.s: This bill would change how Washington taxes cigarettes, vapor products, and other nicotine products. It would set a tax on the sale, handling, or distribution of nicotine products at 95% of the taxable sales price. The bill would also direct money from vapor product taxes into the state general fund and into two other state accounts.

WA-2025-SB6132.s: A narrow group of port districts in Washington would be allowed to take on a little more debt, borrow money, or sell bonds without voter approval if they meet set size rules and have created a tax increment finance area. The extra money must be used for public improvements. The law was signed on March 20, 2026, and takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6132.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6132 HBA LG 26, 2026-02-23)

WA-2025-SB6134.s: The law requires the Employment Security Department to tell workers who apply for strike-related unemployment benefits that they may owe money back if they later get back pay. The notice can be given in the online form, by letter, or another reasonable way. It became law and takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6134.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6134 HBA LAWS 26, 2026-02-23)

WA-2025-SB6136.s: The law requires the state labor and industries agency to publish the workers' compensation rate it says is needed for each risk group, along with any limit it places on a rate increase. If the agency caps a rate increase below that level, it must also show the capped classes, what their rates would have been without the cap, and how other classes are affected. The agency must post this information on its website and send it to lawmakers and an advisory committee. It takes effect June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6136.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6136 SBR LC OC 26, 2026-01-30)

WA-2025-SB6137.s: Allows sports betting on college games in Washington, but not bets on how one college athlete will do. It also lets tribal gaming compacts be changed to allow sports betting on Indian lands, and lets a bet placed over the internet be accepted at a tribe’s gaming facility if the customer is physically there. Became law and takes effect June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6137.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6137 SBR BTE OC 26, 2026-01-28)

WA-2025-SB6148.s: Regional transit authorities would be able to issue general obligation or revenue bonds with terms up to 75 years. If an authority issues a bond with a term longer than 40 years, it would not be eligible for regional mobility grant program funds. This affects regional transit authorities and the grant money they can receive.
WA-2025-SB6148.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6148 SBR TRAN OC 26, 2026-02-06)

WA-2025-SB6149.s: The law changes which counties count as rural for public facilities funding. A county with at least 100 people per square mile and no city over 45,000 people is now included. It became Chapter 42, 2026 Laws, and takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6149.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6149-S SBR FBR 26, 2026-03-30)

WA-2025-SB6151.s: The law creates a new Laboratory Accreditation Account for fees Ecology charges environmental labs for lab accreditation. It also sends fees for landfill methane emissions to the Air Pollution Control Account. These accounts would pay Ecology’s costs for those programs. It became law and takes effect on 6/11/2026.
WA-2025-SB6151.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6151 HBR APP 26, 2026-03-02)

WA-2025-SB6160.s: This bill would change some reporting requirements for state agencies, the Washington student achievement council, and the Washington state board of education. It would eliminate some reports, change how often some reports are filed, and allow some information to be made public in other ways instead of through reports. It also changes reporting and compliance rules for covered building owners under the state energy performance standard.

WA-2025-SB6161.s: The bill would require Washington’s health department to consider adding plain information about lowering dementia risk to public health campaign materials when research links the topic to dementia risk. It would also ask the department to consider adding dementia risk and diagnosis information to health care provider materials and public websites when there is a research link. Any updated materials with this information would need to be available in all languages the department already uses, and the department would consult dementia experts when preparing provider or public information.
WA-2025-SB6161.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6161 SBA HLTC 26, 2026-01-20)

WA-2025-SB6162.s: This law changes property tax relief for retired persons by expanding and streamlining the exemption program. It also consolidates the state property tax and makes the use of state property tax revenue more transparent. The changes affect qualifying homeowners, including some seniors, people retired because of disability, some veterans, and certain surviving spouses or domestic partners.

WA-2025-SB6170.s: The law raises the dollar limits for some Washington state highway work and contracts. It lets state crews do more highway construction and repair work before outside bidding is needed, including a higher limit during emergencies. It also raises the limit for some transportation department contracts meant to help small, veteran, minority, and women-owned businesses compete.
WA-2025-SB6170.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6170 SBA TRAN 26, 2026-01-26)

WA-2025-SB6178.s: The bill would stop people from getting an insured person to sign away post-loss property insurance benefits, and any such agreement would be void. It would mainly affect property insurance policyholders and people who provide repair, restoration, or similar services after a loss. The state insurance commissioner could order someone to stop, seek a court order, and fine them $50,000 for each violation.
WA-2025-SB6178.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6178 SBR APS0 26, 2026-02-05)

WA-2025-SB6182.s: The law creates a grant program to help keep abortion clinical care available in Washington. The Health Secretary can give operating grants to certain providers and organizations to help people who are uninsured, underinsured, or cannot safely use their insurance for abortion care. It also limits the health department from collecting or sharing identifying details about people who get help or about staff who provide this care, except when needed to run the program.
WA-2025-SB6182.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6182-S2 SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-16)

WA-2025-SB6183.s: Health plans in Washington, including plans for public employees, must cover all FDA-approved HIV antiviral drugs for plans issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2027. The plans cannot use prior approval, step therapy, or other use limits for those drugs. If the FDA has approved several similar versions of a drug, the plan does not have to cover every version if at least one similar version is covered without those limits. It became law as Chapter 48, 2026 Laws, and takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6183.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6183-S SBR FBR 26, 2026-03-31)

WA-2025-SB6184.s: The bill would change several state programs that help homeless youth and young adults. It would adjust shelter notice rules, rename one housing program, remove some county and end-date limits, and change who can get help and how funds can be used. It would also update legal terms and agency names used in these programs.
WA-2025-SB6184.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6184-S HBR APP 26, 2026-03-03)

WA-2025-SB6188.s: The law lets the Washington Department of Labor and Industries make rules about asbestos training and certification without being limited to only the rules needed to match federal law. It affects asbestos certification rules in Washington. It became law on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6188.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6188 SBR HA 26, 2026-03-03)

WA-2025-SB6189.s: Washington law changes the deadline for certain local governments to create an extra public facilities district for regional aquatics and sports facilities. It applies to two or more neighboring towns or cities, or those towns or cities plus the county or counties where they are located, if they helped create a public facilities district before. The law takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6189.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6189-S SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-01)

WA-2025-SB6194.s: Starting July 1, 2026, hospitals on federally recognized Indian reservations can be paid based on their allowable costs for inpatient and outpatient Medicaid care. This does not include beds in the psychiatric unit. The bill became law as Chapter 124, 2026 Laws, with an effective date of June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6194.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6194 SBR WM TA 26, 2026-02-04)

WA-2025-SB6197.s: Washington changed the rules for suspending a plumbing license. A person would need five violations in five years, instead of three in 36 months, before a suspension can be ordered, and the advisory board no longer has to recommend it. The labor department must also give regular updates on enforcement actions to the plumbing advisory board. The law takes effect on 1/1/2027.
WA-2025-SB6197.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6197-S.E HBA LAWS 26, 2026-02-23)

WA-2025-SB6200.s: The law lets renters and mobile home occupants install portable cooling devices, like a window air conditioner or portable heat pump, in most cases. Landlords can block or limit them only for set safety, code, damage, power, egress, or insurance reasons, and they may require drainage or inspection for window units. It became law and takes effect on 6/11/2026.
WA-2025-SB6200.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6200-S.E SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-15)

WA-2025-SB6210.s: The bill would change how the Washington Exchange sets yearly rules for certifying health plans sold on the Exchange Market. It would require the Exchange to review market conditions and use measurable criteria that can look at things like plan cost, benefits, premiums, drug lists, provider networks, and quality. For plan year 2028 and later, it would also set a timeline for early notice, public comment, final notice, and any later updates to those criteria.
WA-2025-SB6210.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6210-S.E HBA HCW 26, 2026-02-19)

WA-2025-SB6220.s: Nonprofit housing providers with the low-income homeownership property tax exemption could keep that exemption if the property is temporarily rented or loaned to another group for certain community uses, as long as the bill’s conditions are met. The exemption would also not end if the property is transferred to another nonprofit for a use that still qualifies. These nonprofits would have to file an annual renewal declaration by March 31 to keep the tax break.
WA-2025-SB6220.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6220 SBR APS 26, 2026-02-17)

WA-2025-SB6222.s: School districts and educational service districts could sell or give away extra school tech, like laptops and tablets, to public school students. Students from low-income families would get first priority, and they could receive the items at no cost. Any sale or gift would have to be put in a written agreement that shows the item’s used value, if any.
WA-2025-SB6222.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6222 SBR EDU OC 26, 2026-02-04)

WA-2025-SB6225.s: The law authorizes up to $800 million in state bonds for highway design, land, and construction work, and puts the money into the Move Ahead Washington Account. It also raises the bond limit for State Route 520 by $500 million, to $2.45 billion. The bonds are paid first from fuel taxes and vehicle fees, and some unused bond authority ends June 30, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6225.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6225-S SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-20)

WA-2025-SB6226.s: Licensed audiologists and other licensed professionals may use their own clinical judgment to choose telehealth or in-person care when fitting and dispensing hearing devices and communication devices. The state board still keeps its power to set and enforce rules on care standards, supervision, records, equipment checks, consumer notices, and safety follow-up, and the law takes effect June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6226.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6226-S SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-15)

WA-2025-SB6228.s: The law removes a lower business and occupation tax rate for warehousing and reselling prescription drugs. Starting January 1, 2027, those businesses will pay a 0.5% tax on that income instead of 0.138%. It applies to businesses that buy prescription drugs from a manufacturer or another wholesaler and resell them to retailers or health care providers.
WA-2025-SB6228.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6228 SBR WM TA 26, 2026-02-18)

WA-2025-SB6231.s: Beginning July 1, 2026, the state would stop giving new tax exemption certificates to some data centers that qualify through refurbishment. It would also end the sales and use tax break for replacement server equipment. Data centers refurbished on or after July 1, 2026, in counties with more than 800,000 people would not qualify for the exemption.
WA-2025-SB6231.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6231-S.E SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-20)

WA-2025-SB6237.s: Landlords in Washington would have to tell tenants if a rental may be in a flood hazard area or other flood-prone area. They would also have to say that the landlord’s insurance does not cover a tenant’s personal items and that tenants should think about renter’s insurance and flood insurance. The notice would also point tenants to county information about flood and other property hazards, and it would apply only to leases signed after December 31, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6237.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6237-S SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-16)

WA-2025-SB6239.s: This bill would create a claims commission in the office of administrative hearings to handle tort claims against the state, its political subdivisions, and certain officers, employees, or volunteers. Some personal injury claims would have to go to the commission before a lawsuit can be filed, while other claims could be filed in the commission or in court. The bill sets up an expedited examiner track and a hearing track, with filing fees, hearings, written decisions, and rules for appeals to superior court. It also requires reports on large awards and a later review of the commission’s work.

WA-2025-SB6244.s: This law extends a hazardous substance tax exemption for certain agricultural crop protection products that are warehoused in Washington or transported to or from the state. The products must be used only by a farmer or certified applicator, and the person holding them may not otherwise use, manufacture, package for sale, or sell them in Washington. The law also updates the stated public policy for the exemption and says the legislature may extend the expiration date if a review finds an average increase in hazardous substance tax revenue.

WA-2025-SB6246.s: Changes how Washington tracks and plans emissions for emissions-intensive, trade-exposed facilities under the climate commitment act. It sets rules for Ecology to study future no-cost allowance levels, asks for recommendations by December 1, 2026, and requires certain facility reporting starting in 2028. If lawmakers do not set a future allowance schedule by December 1, 2027, these facilities would keep getting no-cost allowances under the current third compliance period until a new schedule is adopted.
WA-2025-SB6246.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6246 SBR ENET TA 26, 2026-02-02)

WA-2025-SB6247.s: This bill would require educational service districts to give extra budget help to school districts that show signs of financial distress or enter binding conditions. It would also require school board members to take training on school funding and finance, and it would let districts ask for and share records about knowing violations before hiring people for budget or accounting jobs. The bill also sets reporting duties for suspected financial wrongdoing and updates rules on school district spending limits.

WA-2025-SB6248.s: The law creates the Washington Travel Insurance Act and sets rules for selling travel insurance in the state. It lets the Insurance Commissioner issue a special license for travel insurance sellers and requires travel retailers to be licensed or registered. It also requires sellers to give buyers key policy details, keep a list of travel retailers, and follow the same penalty rules that apply to other insurance producers.
WA-2025-SB6248.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6248-S HBR APP 26, 2026-03-03)

WA-2025-SB6258.s: The Washington Medical Commission would be allowed to make rules for doctors, physician assistants, and certified anesthesiologist assistants to give up their licenses on a voluntary, nonpunitive path. It would also cover some licenses under two interstate licensing compacts. A person could not use this process if they are facing discipline or an investigation, and giving up the license would end the right to renew or get it back.
WA-2025-SB6258.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6258 SBR HLTC OC 26, 2026-01-30)

WA-2025-SB6260.s: This law changes how some public school programs are funded and managed in Washington. It sets new rules for school bus payment timelines, changes Running Start funding limits, and gives OSPI new rules for who gets priority in transition to kindergarten funding and how those slots are reported. It also lets some schools charge sliding-scale fees for transition to kindergarten and changes how special education and local effort aid are counted for certain students and districts.
WA-2025-SB6260.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6260-S.E SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-20)

WA-2025-SB6262.s: For vehicles that already pay gross weight license fees, the bill would raise the maximum weight for a transportation benefit district vehicle fee to 9,000 pounds. It would affect heavier vehicles in Washington that fall under those fees.
WA-2025-SB6262.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6262-S.E HBR TR 26, 2026-03-03)

WA-2025-SB6268.s: The Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction must keep an online public record of final decisions on special education community complaints. Each decision must be free to view and stay online for 20 years after the complaint is finished. If the office does not have 20 years of older records by the effective date, it must post the longest record it has. The bill became law and takes effect on 6/11/2026.
WA-2025-SB6268.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6268-S HBR APH 26, 2026-03-03)

WA-2025-SB6269.s: The law updates the state’s motor fuel rules to include certain gas-based fuels used to power motor vehicles or for transportation. It also removes biodiesel from that definition because it has its own one. The separate definition of alternative fuel is removed. It became law and takes effect on June 11, 2026.
WA-2025-SB6269.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6269-S SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-13)

WA-2025-SB6278.s: The law changes how Washington reviews approved teacher and principal training programs. It requires the state board to look at program standards, educator role standards, program evidence, and input from teachers, schools, and other local partners, and to update those parts as classroom needs and state or federal rules change. After each review, the board must tell a program what needs to change and require a plan to get back in line. Starting January 1, 2027, student teacher field placement plans must be sent in on a schedule set by the board, at least once every three years.
WA-2025-SB6278.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6278 HBR APH 26, 2026-03-03)

WA-2025-SB6289.s: The bill would require the department to develop a statewide economic development and competitiveness strategic plan. The plan would include goals and strategies for state-supported economic development, a state economic profile, economic challenges and opportunities, updates on the small business resiliency program and other business programs, equity and community wealth building efforts, metrics, and an implementation plan. It would be completed by June 30, 2027, updated every two years, and delivered to the appropriate legislative committees.

WA-2025-SB6291.s: Local health boards may let some unlicensed workers review designs and inspect on-site wastewater treatment systems if they work under a certified person’s supervision. That can last for up to four years after the worker is hired.
WA-2025-SB6291.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6291 SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-15)

WA-2025-SB6297.s: Temporary staffing services sold to nonprofit behavioral health entities would be exempt from retail sales tax. The income from those services would still be taxed under the service tax rule instead of the retail tax rule. This would affect staffing firms that provide temporary workers and nonprofit behavioral health providers.
WA-2025-SB6297.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6297 SBR APS2 26, 2026-03-03)

WA-2025-SB6302.s:
This law requires the Department of Labor and Industries to investigate possible misclassification of independent contractors on public works projects when a contractor or subcontractor uses three or more independent contractors for the same type of covered finishing work at the same time. Covered finishing work includes drywall, flooring, tiling, painting, and glazier and glasswork.

A referral for investigation can come from the public agency awarding the contract, a contractor or subcontractor on the project, a labor organization, or an individual doing the work. If misclassification is found, the contractor or subcontractor is subject to the requirements, liabilities, and penalties under state law, and the department must make the proper referrals under Titles 50 and 51 RCW.

WA-2025-SB6309.s: This law gives regional transit authorities new permit options for their facilities. They may apply for land use, construction, and technical permits before they own the property or before a local government makes a land use decision, if they give notice to the property owner. Local governments may also issue permits for work on property the transit authority does not own, and they must accept permit applications from a regional transit authority if the application is otherwise complete. The law also allows rail fixed guideway facilities to exceed local height limits and setback requirements if the authority complies with those rules to the extent practicable.

WA-2025-SB6311.s: This bill would require continuous, accessible pedestrian passage during certain construction work in hospital impact zones, public park impact zones, school speed zones, and school walk zones. It would generally bar sidewalk closures in those areas unless no feasible same-side route or other practical way to keep passage exists, and it would require temporary pedestrian routes to meet accessibility standards. Permit holders would have to submit a pedestrian access safety plan, and the permitting authority could inspect the work zone, order corrections, issue stop work orders, assess civil penalties, or revoke the permit for repeated violations.

WA-2025-SB6313.s: The bill would create a new state account for Capitol Centennial Stewardship. Statewide elected officials, including lawmakers, could ask for gifts, grants, and donations for the account, and the money could be used only after lawmakers approve spending it for capitol repairs, educational work, and projects that help the public take part in state government. The account and the gift-soliciting rule would end on June 30, 2033, and any money left on July 1, 2033 would move to another state account.
WA-2025-SB6313.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6313 SBR SGTE TA 26, 2026-02-02)

WA-2025-SB6323.s: The bill would expand LEOFF 2 duty-related death benefits for surviving spouses of line-of-duty deaths. It would add reimbursement for Medicare Part A and B premiums, and it would also cover some medical premiums paid between a member’s death and the finding that the death happened on the job. The Medicare premium payments would apply after the act’s effective date, and the other premium reimbursements would apply to payments made after June 10, 2010.
WA-2025-SB6323.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6323 SBR WM TA 26, 2026-02-08)

WA-2025-SB6343.s: This bill would change Washington property tax rules for property damaged in a natural disaster in an area declared a disaster area. It would reduce the assessed value of damaged property and allow taxes on that reduction to be abated or refunded. It would also give a tax exemption for certain improvements to qualifying single-family dwellings damaged by a natural disaster. The changes would apply to taxes levied for collection in 2027 and later.

WA-2025-SB6346.s: It became law and would add a 9.90% tax on Washington taxable income for individuals, starting January 1, 2028, with first payments and returns in 2029. It would also allow a $1 million standard deduction per person, with a combined $1 million limit for spouses or domestic partners, and a charitable deduction of up to $100,000 per person. The law would mainly affect people with high income in Washington.
WA-2025-SB6346.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6346-S.E SBR HA 26, 2026-03-11)

WA-2025-SB6347.s: This law changes Washington’s estate tax rules. It sets the estate tax exclusion amount at different levels for deaths before July 1, 2026, on or after July 1, 2026, and for 2027 and later. It also changes the tax rate tables for estates based on the value of the Washington taxable estate.

WA-2025-SB6351.s: The bill would exempt some sales tax on certain services bought by elementary and secondary schools, school districts, and educational service districts, like software work, website help, tech support, security, staffing, ads, and live presentations. It would also treat before-and-after school care programs and classes from arts and cultural nonprofit groups as not being live presentations, so sales tax would not apply to those sales. The bill would also tax that income under the services tax category instead of the retail tax category.
WA-2025-SB6351.src: Washington Legislature Senate bill report (6351-S SBR APS 26, 2026-03-03)

WA-2025-SB6354.s: The law lets some battery-electric vehicle makers own and run a dealership in Washington if they meet set rules, including having no past dealer franchise deals and already having a service site in the state. It also sets rules and fines for unlawful vehicle sales or leases by manufacturers that are not allowed to act as dealers. The fee for a new or used vehicle title application goes from $15 to $40 from October 1, 2026, through December 31, 2036, and some of that money goes to electric vehicle programs.
WA-2025-SB6354.src: Washington Legislature final bill report (6354-S.E SBR FBR 26, 2026-04-15)

WA-2025-SB6355.s: Creates the Washington Electric Transmission Authority, a state public body focused on electric transmission. The authority would work to improve electric service by helping build and upgrade power lines, working with utilities and other groups, and supporting projects that connect renewable power and regional markets. It could also use tools like contracts, grants, federal loans, and, if needed, land take for new transmission corridors after trying to buy the land first.
WA-2025-SB6355.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (6355-S HBA APP 26, 2026-03-04)

WA-2025-SB6362.s: This bill changes rules for court hearings, especially protection order cases and interpreter services. It expands when hearings may be held in person or remotely, and it sets rules for remote access, recordings, and privacy. It also changes how courts appoint interpreters and requires more standards, training, and credentialing for spoken language interpreters.

WA-2025-SCR8408.s: This resolution would reintroduce bills, joint resolutions, joint memorials, and concurrent resolutions from the 2025 regular session in the house where they started. It says those measures would keep the same number and keep the highest status they reached in their original house. It applies to measures introduced in the 2025 regular session of the 69th Legislature.

WA-2025-SCR8409.s: This resolution says the Washington Legislature’s 2026 Regular Session should adjourn sine die. It applies to the Senate and the House of Representatives concurring.

WA-2025-SCR8410.s: This resolution sets rules for what each chamber must do with bills and resolutions that were not passed before adjournment sine die. It says the Senate must send unpassed House measures to the House Rules Committee, and the House must send unpassed Senate measures to the Senate Rules Committee. It also says the Senate secretary and House chief clerk must keep certain measures and related records, and that measures in any special session will be numbered as a continuation of the 2026 regular session.

WA-2025-SJM8006.s: This resolution asks the state Supreme Court to restart the limited license legal technician program and begin issuing new licenses again. It also asks for the program to expand within one year so these technicians can help at some administrative hearings and with eviction and debt cases. It would also form a work group to study how they could help people charged with offenses in lower-level courts and to make recommendations within two years.
WA-2025-SJM8006.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (8006 HBR CRJ 26, 2026-02-27)

WA-2025-SJM8014.s: This memorial asks the United States to open a transparent, thorough, and independent investigation into the violent death of Ayseñur Ezgi Eygi. It says the request is meant to ensure justice and accountability for Eygi and for other United States citizens killed under the jurisdiction of a foreign government.

WA-2025-SJM8015.s: The Legislature asks Congress to make sure federal wildfire response agencies have the staff and ability to protect communities, buildings, natural resources, and watersheds, and to keep wildland firefighters safe. It also calls for the federal wildfire service consolidation to be fully staffed and working by April 1, 2026, with no further reorganization until fire activity eases. The request says the unification should be done carefully to avoid cutting firefighting capacity.
WA-2025-SJM8015.src: Washington Legislature House bill report (8015 HBA AGNR 26, 2026-02-16)
